drills.a: Competitive rivalry, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of substitutes, threat of new entrants.

drills.q: Name the four stages of Wardley's evolution axis.
Why isn't 'we use a specific top-tier foundation model' a competitive moat?
drills.a: The foundation-model layer is at product stage, moving toward commodity with multiple competing providers and standardizing interfaces -- a competitor can switch to or already use an equivalent model just as easily. Real advantage has to live in a harder-to-replicate layer like process power or switching costs.

drills.q: A team claims 'our data' is a moat. What three things do you check before accepting that claim?
drills.a: Whether the data is rights-cleared (legally exclusive), whether it's genuinely proprietary (not derivable from corpora foundation models already trained on), and whether it's refreshed faster than a competitor could re-derive an equivalent dataset -- a one-time head start isn't a durable cornered resource.

drills.q: Why is process power specifically underestimated by teams that build 'AI wrapper' products?
drills.a: The visible product (prompt, UI) is genuinely trivial to copy in a weekend, making the whole thing look easy to replicate. But 99%+ reliable production accuracy on a mission-critical task requires years of edge-case engineering and eval infrastructure a fast-follower can't shortcut just by copying the visible surface.

drills.q: What build-vs-buy rule follows from Wardley's evolution axis, and why does the DIRECTION a component is moving matter as much as its current stage?
drills.a: Build at genesis, build/evaluate at custom-built, buy at product stage, rent at commodity. Direction matters because a component moving fast toward commodity is a bad multi-year custom-build bet even if buying looks marginally pricier today -- you'd lock in custom-maintenance cost for something about to become nearly free (e.g. banking's custom core-systems investment 2010-2020 while that category moved toward product stage).

drills.q: A B2B SaaS company with 200 customers claims 'network effects' as their moat. How do you stress-test this?
drills.a: Ask what specific mechanism makes the product better for existing users as new users join -- a real network effect needs that mechanism, not just 'more users, more data, presumably better.' At small B2B scale, most such claims are actually switching-cost claims (integration depth, accumulated config) mislabeled as network effects -- a real but different power with a different investment thesis.

drills.q: Your team wants to platform-ize your agent-orchestration layer for third parties to build on. What two things do you check before investing?
drills.a: Whether there's actual evidenced third-party demand to build on it (not a hunch), and whether the underlying capability is differentiated enough (not racing toward commodity, e.g. against maturing open-source orchestration frameworks) to anchor real ecosystem value -- platform-izing carries real ongoing costs (API stability, backward compat, third-party support) that aren't worth paying without both.

drills.q: Compare Porter's Five Forces and Helmer's 7 Powers -- when do you use each in a real strategy conversation?
drills.a: Porter operates at the industry level: how attractive is this space to compete in, given structural forces mostly outside any one company's control. Helmer operates at the company level: given you're in this space, what specific durable mechanism protects your margin from competitors. Use Porter when deciding whether to enter a market; use Helmer once you're in it, to decide what to actually invest engineering effort in building.

drills.q: Build the strategic argument for why an AI feature should exist, using Porter, Helmer, and Wardley together -- and then argue the opposite.
drills.a: FOR: name which of the five forces the feature shifts in your favor (e.g. raises buyer switching cost, reduces supplier dependence); name the specific Helmer power(s) it builds (most credibly process power and/or switching costs, rarely network effects/branding for B2B AI); place its technical components on a Wardley axis to justify what's built custom vs bought. AGAINST: if it doesn't shift any force, doesn't build a specific power beyond 'we shipped first,' and its core value sits at a rapidly-commoditizing Wardley stage, it's not strategically worth building even if technically impressive.
